title: Greedy Algorithms
relevance: Greedy is a core optimization paradigm in SDE interviews and OAs; candidates must recognize when a local choice is safe and prove it before coding.

phases.goal: Establish what a greedy algorithm is and what properties make a greedy choice globally optimal.

must_hit.point: A greedy algorithm builds a solution piece by piece, always choosing the next piece that offers the most immediate benefit, without reconsidering past choices.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states local best-at-each-step construction and that past choices are never revisited.

must_hit.point: For greedy to yield a globally optimal solution, the problem must exhibit the greedy-choice property and optimal substructure.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names both properties: a local optimum leads to a global optimum, and an optimal solution contains optimal solutions to subproblems.

must_hit.point: To prove a greedy choice is safe in an interview, use an exchange argument: assume an optimal solution that skips the greedy choice, then swap elements to match the greedy solution without worsening the score.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes contradiction-plus-swap: transform a non-greedy optimal into the greedy one without loss, so the greedy choice is always safe.

probes: What two properties must a problem have for a greedy algorithm to be guaranteed optimal?
How do you justify a greedy approach in an interview using an exchange argument?

hints.1: Think about what you decide at each step and whether you ever undo it.
hints.2: Name the two structural properties, then describe assuming a non-greedy optimal and swapping.
hints.3: Greedy-choice property + optimal substructure; exchange: swap until the solution matches greedy without worsening the score.

phases.goal: Show how common greedy patterns actually make and update choices (sort order, range tracking, multi-pass).

must_hit.point: Activity-style scheduling: sort by end time and always pick the next meeting/interval that starts after the current one ends (N Meetings, Non-overlapping Intervals).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says sort by end times, then greedily take the earliest-finishing compatible interval; mentions this is classic activity selection.

must_hit.point: Fractional Knapsack: sort by value-to-weight ratio descending and take as much of the highest-ratio items as possible until capacity is full.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions ratio sort and filling the knapsack with highest bang-for-buck first, allowing fractions.

must_hit.point: Valid Parenthesis String with '*': track a range of possible open counts (low/high); fail if high goes negative; cap low at 0; accept only if low ends at 0.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains min/max open range updates for '(', ')', '*', the high<0 fail, low=max(low,0), and final low==0.

must_hit.point: Candy: initialize all to 1, left-to-right pass for left-neighbor constraints, then right-to-left taking max with right_neighbor+1; a single pass can invalidate earlier left constraints.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes two linear passes and why isolating left then right dependencies needs two passes.

probes: For maximum non-overlapping meetings, what do you sort by and what is the greedy pick?
How does the valid-parenthesis-with-star greedy track possibility without a stack of stars?

hints.1: For intervals, finishing early frees the room for more later.
hints.2: End-time sort + next compatible start; for '*', think range of open counts not a single counter.
hints.3: Sort by end, pick next start after freeTime; low/high open range, high<0 false, low capped at 0, return low==0.

phases.goal: Distinguish when greedy is safe versus when it fails and DP (or another method) is required.

must_hit.point: Greedy often looks right but is wrong: in 0/1 Knapsack, taking most valuable items can waste space and be suboptimal—prove the greedy choice is safe or use DP.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives 0/1 Knapsack as the counterexample and says ask whether the choice is provably safe before committing to greedy.

must_hit.point: Fractional Knapsack makes greedy safe because items can be broken into fractions; without fractions (0/1 Knapsack), the same ratio greedy fails and DP is required.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explicitly contrasts fractional vs 0/1: fractions enable ratio greedy; indivisible items break it.

must_hit.point: Never code a greedy solution until you have mentally verified it with an exchange argument; many look-greedy problems fail on edge cases and need DP.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the interview discipline: prove with exchange before writing code; flags look-greedy → actually DP cases.

probes: Why does value/weight greedy work for Fractional Knapsack but fail for 0/1 Knapsack?
What should you do before committing to a greedy solution in an interview?

hints.1: Ask what changes if you cannot break an item.
hints.2: Fractions preserve ratio optimality; indivisible items can strand capacity.
hints.3: Fractional: ratio greedy is safe; 0/1: greedy can waste space → DP; always exchange-argue first.

phases.goal: Apply greedy templates to classic OA patterns: change-making, jumps, platforms, jobs, intervals.

must_hit.point: Lemonade Change: for a 20 bill, prefer giving one 10 and one 5 over three 5s because 5s are more versatile for future change.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the preferential break for 20 and the reason 5 bills must be conserved.

must_hit.point: Jump Game I: track maxReach; if index exceeds maxReach you are stuck; update maxReach with i+nums[i]. Jump Game II: treat reachable indices as BFS-like levels using currentEnd and farthest, incrementing jumps when i hits currentEnd.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates reachability (maxReach scan) from min jumps (level boundaries currentEnd/farthest).

must_hit.point: Minimum Platforms: sort arrivals and departures independently; sweep—arrival before next departure needs a new platform, departure frees one; track the maximum in use.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes dual-pointer event sweep on sorted arr/dep and max concurrent platforms.

must_hit.point: Job Sequencing: sort jobs by profit descending; assign each to the latest free slot on or before its deadline (each job takes 1 unit of time).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Profit-desc sort + latest-feasible slot before deadline to leave earlier slots open.

probes: On a 20 lemonade payment, which change strategy do you prefer and why?
How do Jump Game I and Jump Game II differ in what the greedy state tracks?

hints.1: Think about which bill denomination you can reuse later.
hints.2: Conserve 5s; for jumps, reach vs jump-count levels.
hints.3: Prefer one 10+one 5 for 20; I: maxReach; II: currentEnd/farthest levels and jump on boundary.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: With fractions, sorting by value-to-weight and taking highest ratio first is safe because a lower-ratio substitute strictly hurts value per unit weight. Without fractions, the same greedy can leave wasted capacity and miss the optimum, so use Dynamic Programming.

Use greedy only when you can prove the greedy-choice property (typically via an exchange argument) and optimal substructure. If you cannot prove the local choice is safe—as with 0/1 Knapsack or other look-greedy edge-case failures—switch to DP.

tradeoffs.topic: N Meetings / activity selection vs Non-overlapping Intervals removals
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Both sort by end time and keep earliest-ending compatible intervals. Maximizing meetings kept is dual to minimizing removals: count kept incompatibles as removals instead of kept meetings.

Left-to-right then right-to-left isolates neighbor constraints and takes max on the second pass. A single pass fails because fixing a right-neighbor constraint can invalidate a previously set left-neighbor relationship.

gotchas.trap: Assuming greedy is correct because the local choice looks optimal (e.g., taking highest-value items in 0/1 Knapsack).
gotchas.correction: Always ask whether the greedy choice is provably safe via an exchange argument; if not, the problem likely needs Dynamic Programming.

gotchas.trap: In Lemonade Change, always breaking a 20 with three 5s.
gotchas.correction: Prefer one 10 and one 5 so remaining 5s stay available for future 10 and 20 customers.

gotchas.trap: In Assign Cookies, giving large cookies to low-greed children first.
gotchas.correction: Satisfy least-greedy children with the smallest valid cookie; a cookie too small for the least greedy child helps no one and should be discarded.

gotchas.trap: Trying to solve Candy constraints in one left-to-right pass.
gotchas.correction: Use two passes: left-to-right for left neighbors, right-to-left taking max with right_neighbor+1 so both sides stay satisfied minimally.

gotchas.trap: Coding a greedy solution before verifying it.
gotchas.correction: Mentally run an exchange argument first; many look-greedy problems fail on edge cases and require DP.
